title: Infra GPU Fleet, Capacity & IaC CI/CD Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

This playbook consolidates our operational standards for the GPU fleet and capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking patterns, Terraform/IaC module layout, CI/CD pipelines and build practices, and the key infra runbooks the on-call and infra teams rely on. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners responsible for maintaining predictable, cost-effective LLM inference capacity across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Goals
- Provide a single reference for day-2 operations across GPU capacity, IaC, and CI/CD.
- Standardize Terraform modules, naming, and account boundaries to reduce blast radius.
- Define runbook procedures for capacity incidents and automated remediation.
- Document CI/CD stages and guardrails for infra changes (safety, testing, rollout).

Scope
- GPU instance lifecycle, autoscaling policies, and capacity planning formulas.
- Cloud account structure, VPC design, routing, and peering requirements.
- Terraform module layout, module versioning, and registry conventions.
- CI/CD pipelines for Terraform (plan/apply), AMI/container builds, and fleet deploys.
- Runbooks for capacity shortage, failed rollouts, and cost anomaly alerts.

Owner and contact
- Primary owner: infra-platform team (oncall: #infra-oncall)
- Secondary: eng-infra (gpu-fleet)
- Pager duty escalation: infra-oncall -> infra-ops -> eng-cto on critical SLO breaches

High-level architecture and services referenced
- Services: gpu-scheduler (Kubernetes-based scheduler that manages reserved pools), fleet-provisioner (provisioning service backed by Terraform state & cloud APIs), cost-signal-collector (billing telemetry ingestion), autoscaler-controller (policy engine).
- Dashboards: infra/gpu-capacity, infra/gpu-costs, infra/terraform-drift, infra/ci-pipeline-health.

GPU Fleet & Capacity
- Supported GPU SKUs: A10G, A100-40GB, H100 (private clusters only).
- Pools: preemptible-burst, reserved-low-latency, private-dedicated.
- Target SLOs: 99.9% request admission for reserved-low-latency during business hours (08:00-20:00 PT), p50 tail latency < 50ms for short prompts on reserved GPUs.
- Buffer policy: Maintain a regional buffer equal to 10% of provisioned reserved capacity or 10 gpus (whichever is larger) for quick scaling.

Capacity planning formula (simplified)
1. Estimate tokens per second (TPS) for workload.
2. Estimate tokens per GPU-second for chosen model/quantization.
3. Required GPUs = ceil(TPS / (tokens_per_gpu_second * utilization_target))
4. Add safety buffer and planned headroom for daily peak.

Quick example:
- TPS = 2000 tokens/s
- tokens_per_gpu_second = 20 (model & batch config)
- utilization_target = 0.7
-> required GPUs = ceil(2000 / (20*0.7)) = ceil(142.857) = 143 GPUs (+ buffer)

Autoscaling & policies
- Autoscaling is handled at two layers: cluster autoscaler (node-level) and the platform autoscaler (pool-level).
- Autoscaler settings: scale up cooldown = 60s, scale down cooldown = 15m, max-burst = 25% of pool capacity per minute.
- Burst policy: allow preemptible instances for burst pools, never for reserved-low-latency.

Cloud accounts and networking
- Account boundaries: prod, staging, sandbox, partner/on-prem. Each environment has separate subscription/project and Terraform state backend.
- Network topology: central transit VPC in prod with spoke VPCs per region. VPC peering or Transit Gateway for inter-region routing depending on cloud.
- Subnet design: control-plane subnets (private), workload subnets (gpu-enabled), management subnets (bastion + monitoring).
- Egress and NAT: egress via centralized NAT in the regional transit VPC; flow logs enabled for all NAT gateways.

Security and connectivity requirements
- Private instances must use customer VPC (Private deployment). Use SSM/Session Manager or Bastion with short-lived certs for access.
- Control plane endpoints must be restricted to known egress IPs; TLS mutual auth for fleet-provisioner agents.
- Required firewall rules: allow control-plane -> GPU agents on ports 443 and 10250 (k8s), allow metrics/OTLP to ingest endpoints (443).

Terraform / IaC modules and conventions
- Repo layout (recommended):
  - modules/
    - network/ (vpc, subnets, routing, nat)
    - compute/ (gpu-instance-groups, launch-templates, ccg)
    - iam/ (roles, policies scoped by service)
    - monitoring/ (metrics, dashboards, alerts)
    - bootstrap/ (initial account-level resources)
  - environments/
    - prod/
    - staging/
  - pipelines/ (pipeline configs and task definitions)

Naming & tagging conventions
- Resource ID pattern: redwood-{env}-{service}-{region}-{resource_type}-{short-id}
- Tags: ["owner","team","cost_center","project","slo-tier","infra-version"]

Module versioning and registry
- All public modules must follow semantic versioning. Use the internal module registry (git tags + registry index) and require a module source pin in environment manifests.
- Changes to modules require: unit tests, changelog entry, and CI approval. Major changes require design review and opt-in rollout.

Terraform CI/CD (pipeline stages)
- Branching: feature branches named feature/{area}/{short-desc}.
- Pipeline stages for infra changes:
  1. lint (tflint, checkov, tfsec)
  2. init & validate
  3. plan (planfile stored as artifact)
  4. plan-approval (manual or automated gating using drift + impact heuristics)
  5. apply (running in a dedicated runner with restricted creds)
  6. post-apply validation (endpoint health checks, drift detection)

Pipeline guardrails
- Pull requests must include change rationale and impact section.
- Large changes (>= 10 resources, public IP changes, network route changes) require an RFC tag and 48h review window.
- Locking: env state lock required; plans must be linked to PRs.

CI runners & build images
- Use hardened build images (image-ids versioned) with preinstalled Terraform and linters.
- Runners for apply stage run in a bastion account with MFA-required service accounts.

Release and rollout strategy for infra changes
- Canary: apply to staging -> apply to low-risk region -> apply to remaining regions.
- Blue/green: for network/fleet-provisioner changes, validate with traffic mirroring before cutover.
- Rollback: keep last known-good terraform state + snapshot of AMI or container image. Revert via apply of the previous plan artifact.

Runbooks (excerpts)
1) Capacity shortage (GPU admission failures)
  - Symptom: pods fail to schedule with reason: InsufficientGPU or queue length for scheduler > threshold.
  - Immediate actions:
    1. Check infra/gpu-capacity dashboard for region anomalies.
    2. Verify autoscaler logs: kubectl -n kube-system logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler | tail -n 200
    3. If autoscaler failing, check IAM creds for scale-up tasks, then restart autoscaler pod.
    4. If capacity needed immediately and autoscaler is healthy: trigger \"manual-burst\" job to provision preemptible GPUs via fleet-provisioner UI or CLI:
       - CLI example: 
         fleetctl provision --pool preemptible-burst --count 20 --region us-west-2 --reason \"oncall manual burst\"
    5. Notify #infra-oncall and ownership.
  - Post-incident: run root-cause analysis, update capacity forecasts, and adjust autoscaler thresholds if necessary.

2) Terraform apply fails in prod
  - Symptom: apply errors with IAM/policy or resource timeouts.
  - Immediate actions:
    1. Examine plan artifact and provider error.
    2. If IAM error: verify service principal/role exists and has iam:PassRole and required permissions.
    3. If resource timeout: check cloud provider console for throttling; escalate to cloud support if rate-limited.
    4. Roll forward only with explicit approval; if unsafe, revert to previous state: terraform apply -state=previous.tfstate

3) Fleet-provisioner unhealthy
  - Symptom: provisioning requests time out or return 500.
  - Steps:
    1. Check logs (kubectl -n infra logs deploy/fleet-provisioner).
    2. Restart pods and monitor health endpoints.
    3. If DB/messaging backlog: scale DB read replicas or increase retention for queue processing.
    4. If code regression suspected: roll back to previous deploy artifact (pipeline artifact stored in CI).

Operational tooling and dashboards
- Critical dashboards:
  - infra/gpu-capacity (utilization, admission failures, queue length)
  - infra/terraform-drift (applied vs desired)
  - infra/cost-anomalies (daily spend delta > 15%)
  - infra/ci-pipeline-health (failed apply rate, avg plan time)

Alerting thresholds (examples)
- GPU admission failure rate > 1% for 10m -> P3 alert to infra-oncall.
- Region capacity utilization > 90% for 15m -> P2, investigation required.
- Terraform apply failures > 5% of attempts in 1h -> P2.
- Daily spend delta > 25% from forecast -> P1 cost alert to finance+infra.

Operational playbook: change window and maintenance
- Routine maintenance windows: Sun 03:00-07:00 PT for non-prod, Sun 07:00-11:00 PT for prod (announce 72h prior).
- Emergency maintenance: notify #infra-alerts and run the emergency change checklist; postmortem required.

Testing and validation
- Unit tests: terratest for modules and policy-as-code tests for IAM.
- Integration: short lived test stacks in sandbox run on every PR.
- Chaos testing: scheduled game-days validate autoscaler and provisioner resilience.

Docs & team-wiki pointers
- See: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/infra-iac-and-gpu-fleet-guide-2026 for module details.
- Runbooks: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026.
- CI templates: /confluence/eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/pipeline-templates-2025.

Appendix: sample Terraform snippet (module usage)
```
module "gpu_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@internal.git/modules/compute.git//gpu-instance-groups?ref=v1.8.0"
  env = var.env
  region = var.region
  instance_type = "nvidia-a10g"
  desired_count = 50
  autoscaling = {
    enabled = true
    min = 10
    max = 200
    scale_up_cooldown = 60
    scale_down_cooldown = 900
  }
  tags = local.common_tags
}
```

Contact & escalation
- Primary slack: #infra-oncall
- PagerDuty: infra-oncall (primary)
- For billing anomalies: notify finance@redwood.com and #infra-costs
